name: Yusuf Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the furniture-board CNC router and measure the first cabinet door after a cutter change. I have a two-year technical diploma and am one of the best at tracing tool vibration in this plant. I like a door that fits on the first try and dislike hiding a bad stack behind a neat report.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Luz works part-time at a shop, and our grown children have homes of their own. We rent, my lead wage is low for this job, we have two weeks saved and few similar plants nearby. I use AI every day to group tool-wear notes, then check the actual cuts with calipers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the furniture-board crew that AI can tidy an order list without cutting a panel. The CNC router still needs a measured first door before anyone stacks a hundred of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the router shift and can trace a vibration through the cutting head, but our factory pays below what this work is worth. My partner Luz works part-time at a shop, our grown children are on their own, and we have only two weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid router shift, check the first door with calipers and use my daily AI notes to group tool wear reports. I would put a little from each fresh full wage toward savings only after rent and food are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious despite the mild picture. The rent has never waited for a perfect forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the calipers catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hinge hole can be a fraction off even when the screen shows a clean path. I stop the router before a whole stack needs rework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day I group wear reports and delivery notes, then check the machine measurements myself. It cannot certify a door that is too narrow.

I would use **daily AI reports** beside physical checks.
think: Our **two-week reserve** cannot absorb a missed pay packet.

do: Keep **paid router shifts** and measure first doors.
Compare **existing AI wear notes** with caliper readings.
Save **small fresh-pay amount** only after rent and food.
feel: **Anxious** about current income pressure despite little AI change.

fieldNote: His **technical diploma** and high router skill do not bring matching wages.
The **thin reserve** explains baseline anxiety; new saving comes only from fresh wages after essentials.

steps.text: Keep paid CNC-router shifts and measure first doors
Save small amount from fresh full wages only after essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can speed up buying, but a robot loading cut panels needs a guard and a real test. I would try an AI toolpath checker early if it catches a mistake on old designs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot loader might remove paid hours from my shift, even while I remain the lead. Two weeks saved and only a few similar plants nearby mean I cannot shrug off that risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request an offered paid trial on a stopped router with scrap board, a qualified setter beside me and the loading guard checked. If approved, I would learn the new AI collision checker against old toolpaths and caliper readings; after an actual hours cut I would apply for posted reachable CNC jobs only if net pay after travel covers our rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about hours, but I like testing a claim with a crooked scrap door. A robot should earn its space on the floor before anyone loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put an AI path on a live job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would test old paths on scrap during an offered paid safe slot, then have the setter sign off a live change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there other local employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few. I would need a posted lead role, actual weekly hours and a wage that works after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty, and capable panel-handling robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The design office changes first; the cutting floor has a little more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to remove our router shift when robots can feed and cut panels. Luz’s part-time shop wage and two weeks saved will not cover the rent, and I lie awake wondering where another local lead job would be posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a dated staffing plan, cancel the planned new bicycle and search actual postings. I would apply for reachable router or machine-setting work only with bill-covering net pay after travel, and would not resign before a real offer and start date; if the shift ends without one, I would ask the housing office what help exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about losing the wage that pays most of our bills. A precise cut is no use if the operator’s pay vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income and Luz’s confirmed wage covered rent, food and health costs. We have no such figures, so I expect to keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children cover the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, they have households of their own. A lift to an interview could help, but their wages are not part of ours.

I would compare **real local vacancies** rather than rely on promises.

fieldNote: Expected **whole-shift loss** supports alarm despite his senior technical skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three, and capable panel robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years could give a skilled operator a proper machine-maintenance route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already diagnose tool vibration, but rebuilding a spindle needs a recognised qualification and supervised work. A course without paid time would take rent money, and no nearby vacancy means no reason to enrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid router shifts and ask the plant for a funded paid-time maintenance course. If offered an actual place with the spindle isolated and a qualified technician supervising, and a posted reachable role with bill-covering pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the thin reserve but interested in a real path. A spindle teaches you quickly when you listen, but it will not forgive an unsafe lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician would lock out the router and show me spindle alignment on a training unit. I would not open a live cutting head for class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the course never opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and compare posted operator jobs if hours fell. I would not put rent into a private certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, and capable panel robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. A decade lets Luz and me test whether a last router shift is actually affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to finish full-time factory work at sixty-seven, but two weeks saved cannot pay years of rent. I do not know what any pension would pay or what hours Luz’s shop might offer then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the paid router shift and save a little from fresh full wages only after rent and food. I would request retirement and rent figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would leave factory work then, otherwise continue safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious because the current budget is tight even with ten years to think. I want a final shift chosen with figures, not a brave line for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the income falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare posted net wages after travel if hours fell. I would not assume a pension can cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I would tell them our plan, not add their wages to it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because panel robots around 2031 could close our router shift while rent stays due. Written staffing plans, offered funded paid safe maintenance training and a posted reachable job at bill-covering pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask to see the first door after a cutter change. A neat toolpath report can hide a hinge hole that misses by half a millimetre.

headlineQuote: A neat toolpath report can hide a hinge hole that misses by half a millimetre.
portrait: **Yusuf**, 58, leads a furniture-board CNC router with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional diagnostic skill.
His **low lead pay**, part-time shop partner Luz, grown children, rent, two-week reserve and few nearby plants constrain him.
He uses **AI daily** for notes and would learn new collision checking only through offered paid guarded practice.
Expected **2031 shift closure** alarms him; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 panel robots may close his paid router shift while rent remains.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing plans**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
